evidence: Ter. Ad. 5.5.3: Quid fit? quid agitur? — Rēctē. (Lewis & Short s.v. regō)
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “esp. in answers, in colloquial lang., well, quite well, right”; also a politely evasive “it’s all right, nothing’s the matter” (Plaut. Merc. 2.3.33: Rēctē, pater).

evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 2.2.11: Rēctē valet? — Vīvit rēctē et valet. (Lewis & Short s.v. regō)
Plaut. Am. 2.1.36: equidem valeō rēctē et salvus sum (Lewis & Short s.v. valeō)
Traupman 17: to be very well, rēctē valēre
Cic. Att. 12.37: bellē sē habēre (Lewis & Short s.v. bellus)
Cic. Fam. 9.9.1: bellē habēre, to be in good health (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The word of Cicero’s letters for being well; the superlative too: bellissimē esse (Cic. Att. 14.14.1, Lewis & Short). Traupman 17 adds Bellissimē and Perbellē, very well; Lewis & Short has perbellē “very finely” (Cic. Fam. 16.18.1) but not of health.

terms.gloss: I’m well, things are going well for me
evidence: Cic. N. D. 1.114; Hor. S. 2.8.19; Catull. 23.5 (Lewis & Short s.v. pulcher)
terms.comment: Impersonal, with the person in the dative: “it is fine for me”.

phrases.latin: «Rēctēne advēnistis?» inquit avia. «Bene habēmus,» inquit pater.
phrases.english: “Did you have a good journey?” said Grandma. “We’re fine,” said Dad.
